facts.claim: GiveWell's models for grants to its Top Charities have typically estimated an average cost between $3,000 and $5,500 to save a life.
facts.quote: Over the past several years, our models for grants to our Top Charities have typically estimated an average cost between $3,000 and $5,500.

source.name: GiveWell, “How Much Does It Cost To Save a Life?”

facts.claim: GiveWell's worked example for one Malaria Consortium grant in Nigeria: $3,000 funds about 2,189 monthly courses of preventive malaria medicine, enough to protect 498 children for the high-transmission season; GiveWell estimates this averts about 1.3 deaths, or about one once it accounts for how other funders respond.
facts.quote: The cost of delivering one monthly course (or "cycle") of treatment is about $1.37, so $3,000 in donations can fund the delivery of about 2,189 cycles of medication. ... 498 children under the age of five will receive treatments for the full high-transmission season. ... In our initial estimate, this donation will avert 1.3 deaths. ... Once we adjust for the impact of that reduced funding, we estimate that this donation will save one life.
facts.asOf: 2024 estimate for a 2023 grant (page published April 2024); GiveWell notes this grant may be more cost-effective than its average grant

source.name: GiveWell, “How Much Does It Cost To Save a Life?”

facts.claim: GiveWell estimates it costs between $3,000 and $8,000 to save a life through the Against Malaria Foundation's net campaigns, 9x to 23x as cost-effective as direct cash transfers.
facts.quote: It costs between $3,000 and $8,000 to save a life in countries where GiveWell currently supports AMF to deliver ITN campaigns. This equates to being 9x to 23x as cost-effective as direct cash transfers (GiveWell’s benchmark for comparing different programs).

facts.claim: GiveWell estimates each insecticide-treated net costs roughly $4 to $6 to buy and distribute, varying by location.
facts.quote: As of December 2023, we estimate that it costs between approximately $4 and $6 (varying by location) to distribute each ITN.

facts.claim: GiveWell estimates it costs approximately $2,000 to $7,000, depending on location, to avert a death through Malaria Consortium's seasonal malaria chemoprevention.
facts.quote: As of December 2023, we estimate that it costs approximately $2,000 to $7,000 (depending on the location) to avert a death in areas where GiveWell supports SMC.
facts.asOf: December 2023 (page published January 2024, last updated April 2024)

facts.claim: GiveWell estimates one monthly course of preventive malaria medicine costs about $1.50 to deliver to a child.
facts.quote: As of December 2023, we estimate that it costs approximately $1.50 to deliver one cycle of SMC to a child in Malaria Consortium-supported programs (varying by country, from $1.40 in Nigeria to $1.81 in Chad).

facts.claim: Insecticide-treated nets reduce child deaths from all causes by 17% compared with no nets, about 5.6 lives saved each year for every 1,000 children protected (95% CI 3.6 to 7.6; high-certainty evidence). The trials were run between 1987 and 2001.
facts.quote: Insecticide-treated nets reduce child mortality from all causes by 17% compared to no nets (rate ratio 0.83, 95% CI 0.77 to 0.89; 5 trials, 200,833 participants, high-certainty evidence). This corresponds to a saving of 5.6 lives (95% CI 3.6 to 7.6) each year for every 1000 children protected with ITNs.

source.name: Pryce J, Richardson M, Lengeler C. Insecticide-treated nets for preventing malaria. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2018, Issue 11. CD000363
source.license: Quoted with citation (abstract via Europe PMC, PMID 30398672)

facts.claim: Among HIV/AIDS interventions in the Disease Control Priorities data, the least effective produces less than 0.1 percent of the value of the most effective.
facts.quote: the least effective HIV/AIDS intervention produces less than 0.1 percent of the value of the most effective.

source.name: Toby Ord, “The Moral Imperative toward Cost-Effectiveness in Global Health”, Center for Global Development, 2013
